text: Course 3 covered the basic mechanics: preview checks an Update Set against the target instance before anything is applied, and commit actually applies the changes. At scale, with several Update Sets moving through a release together, preview and commit surface three real problems a single, simple Update Set almost never shows you.

A missing dependency happens when the Update Set you're previewing references something — a Script Include, a table, a field — that doesn't exist yet on the target, because it actually lives in a different Update Set that hasn't been promoted yet. The instinct to force it through anyway is wrong. The real fix is finding which earlier Update Set contains the missing piece, promoting that one first, then re-running preview on the one that depends on it.

During preview, a specific change can get flagged to be skipped rather than applied. Many teams treat a skipped record as a non-event, since it wasn't flagged as an error. In reality, it deserves the same deliberate review as a collision — what exactly got skipped, and was that actually safe? Skipping something that mattered can leave the target instance subtly broken in a way that won't surface until someone hits that exact path later.

A commit applies an Update Set's changes as a sequence of operations. If that sequence gets interrupted partway through, by a network drop or a session timeout, the target instance can end up with some of the changes applied and others not. That's a genuinely messy state. Resolving it means carefully checking what's actually present on the target against what the Update Set intended, record by record, before deciding whether to re-run, manually finish the rest, or roll back what did apply.

A single Update Set promoted alone rarely hits all three problems at once. A release moving six or more sets through a pipeline is different — a missing dependency in one set can mask what would otherwise be a clean promotion, a skipped record in another can go unnoticed amid everything else being reviewed, and any one of several commits can be the one a network blip interrupts.

Treating preview and commit as a single rubber-stamp step, instead of reviewing each one deliberately, is how a multi-Update-Set release ends up in production with problems nobody caught in time. Next up: a worked lab walking through exactly this kind of multi-set promotion gone sideways.
